How do logistic regression and boosting compare in
performance, fairness, explainability and robustness?
A reproducible empirical basis for methodological discussion

30–45 seconds. The opening question is what a more complex model gains and what trade-offs arise. Compare logistic regression and boosting across the empirical dimensions, then introduce the broader framework proposal. The current findings do not validate the proposed framework or establish a new statistical method.

Data and comparison protocol
The same data, predictors and classification rule
Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026
The holdout remains locked against model selection, tuning and recalibration.

60 seconds. The public UCI dataset contains 30,000 Taiwan records with next-month default as the target. We retained all records. Grouping on the 22 predictors eliminated exact overlap by changing 34 partition assignments. Identical predictors do not prove that two records describe the same person. Final pipelines and preprocessing are frozen. Cross-validation fits temporary models within training only. The holdout had been inspected before locking, which limits confirmatory interpretation.

Boosting ranks default risk better
The ranking advantage has little effect on decisions at the 0.50 threshold
Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026
Accuracy ≈ 81.8%
Default recall ≈ 35%

About 65% of observed defaults
remain undetected.
Holdout point estimates. Intervals and calibration diagnostics are available in the explorer.

60 seconds. ROC-AUC and AP describe ranking, while recall measures detected defaults at the reference threshold. AP is sklearn average precision, not trapezoidal PR-AUC. Logistic regression: AUC 0.7569, AP 0.5270, accuracy 0.8180, recall 0.3545. Boosting: AUC 0.7781, AP 0.5521, accuracy 0.8177, recall 0.3515. Brier score and log loss are lower for boosting. Marginal confidence intervals in the explorer do not constitute a paired model-difference test. No new threshold was selected.

Fairness depends on the metric
Ranking gaps and error-rate gaps address different questions
Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026
95% intervals for the primary signed gaps include zero.
pp = percentage points. The results do not establish an overall fairness winner.

60 seconds. pp means percentage points. Recall and FPR gaps are female minus male. SAFE parity is the unsigned maximum-minus-minimum gap between group RGA values. RGA agrees numerically with AUC in this binary dataset, without implying a universal identity. Boosting has a smaller SAFE gap but larger absolute recall and FPR gaps. Signed intervals include zero, which does not establish equivalence or absence of disparity. A positive prediction flags default risk and does not represent credit approval. Associations between SEX and predictors do not identify causal effects.

Shared leading predictors, different concentration
SHAP complements SAFE RGE with global and individual explanations
Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026
PAY_0 and LIMIT_BAL
lead both models

SHAP / RGE rank correlation
0.918 logistic / 0.927 boosting
SHAP contributions use log-odds and do not represent causal effects.

60 seconds. PAY_0 and LIMIT_BAL lead both models. The top three predictors are PAY_0, LIMIT_BAL and PAY_6 for logistic regression, and PAY_0, LIMIT_BAL and PAY_AMT1 for boosting. SHAP explains default log-odds relative to a shared background of 100 training records. Contributions from 85 transformed columns are summed to 22 predictors. For boosting, this aggregation is not a separate coalition game on raw predictors. Authentic RGE assesses ranking changes after replacing inputs with training references. SHAP already appears in KAIRI and is not a methodological novelty of this project. ID 2 in the explorer is an observed default missed by both models. The fixed local cases are illustrative rather than representative.

title: Robustness depends on the stress scenario

text: Robustness depends on the stress scenario
SAFE tail swaps and semantic corruptions have different exposure levels
Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026
Input exposure: approximately 65% SAFE / 10% semantic.
Semantic: GBM − LR ≈ 0.32 pp, conditional 95% CI ≈ [0.30, 0.34] pp.

preview: Joint stress | Model | RGR | Mean |Δp| | Flag flips

text:
90 seconds. SAFE p=0.05 swaps opposite input tails. The parameter is a tail fraction, not a 5% change to each value. Joint SAFE changes inputs for about 65.14% of holdout records. Semantic q=0.10 selects about 10% and uses rules based on training IQR, age, supported positive repayment delays and conditional categorical substitutions. Special repayment states -2, -1 and 0 remain unchanged. There are 30 semantic repetitions and 167 scenarios with 1,501 realizations overall. Semantic mean absolute probability movement is 0.51 pp for logistic regression and 0.83 pp for boosting. The paired GBM-minus-LR difference is 0.318 pp, with conditional 95% CI [0.297, 0.340] pp. RGR has point estimates only and model-specific normalization. Stress severities are not equivalent, and observed outcomes remain fixed.

Broader framework proposal
Extending SAFE/KAIRI with complementary indicators and associated tests
Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026
Cross-cutting bias and a proposed mapping to EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and HLEG.

60 seconds. This summarizes the colleague’s proposal rather than a validated framework. The document calls for complementary indicators with formulas, associated tests, classification by model access and sources. It proposes uncertainty and calibration as a fifth axis, with bias across dimensions. Mapping to the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and HLEG remains proposed and has not undergone legal validation. The draft uncertainty table repeats explainability rows. This summary follows the explicit intention in the introduction, and the draft needs correction before further development.

Current coverage of the proposal
Completed metrics provide partial coverage of the proposed modules and tests
Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026

preview: Dimension | Implemented | Pending in the proposal

text:
90 seconds. We do not assign a percentage of framework completion. Brier score and log loss are implemented, while DM, DeLong and MCS have not been executed. Group rates, gaps, ratios and bootstrap intervals exist, but the proposed z and permutation tests and entropy indicators do not. Semantic corruptions are distinct from energy distance, MMD and DeepFool. SHAP and RGE do not constitute AOPC, fidelity or randomization testing. Group SHAP comparisons have no formal KS test. Global ECE and conditional intervals are distinct from aleatoric and epistemic decomposition or conformal prediction. Coverage is partial at the level of selected indicators and diagnostics. Broader implementation remains deferred pending professor feedback.

Appendix: uncertainty and reproducibility
Technical details for discussion
APPENDIX / Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026

Appendix for technical questions. Bootstrap uses 2,000 exact-predictor-group resamples with seed 42 and percentile intervals. Groups can cross SEX and outcome categories and remain intact. Both models share resamples. Intervals condition on frozen models and observed data, and robustness also conditions on saved corruption realizations. Within each resample, nonlinear metrics are calculated separately for each semantic repetition and then averaged. SD across 30 repetitions is Monte Carlo variability rather than a sampling interval. Saved robustness verification reports 30 passing tests and 24 CSV files and the prediction cache identical across two runs. The explorer is an offline snapshot generated from saved tables, rather than a live database connection.

Proposed indicators and tests
Partial coverage of indicators and their associated tests
APPENDIX / Credit risk fairness · 9 October 2026

Appendix on indicator coverage. Calculating a score and executing its associated statistical test are distinct steps. Interpretation of flagging ratios depends on the meaning of the positive label. A default-risk ratio does not automatically imply discrimination in loan approvals. Mean predicted probability versus observed event frequency is descriptive and has no t-test. SHAP data are saved, but formal KS and Gini tests have not been run. Proposed tests require review for statistical suitability. MCS, AOPC and conformal prediction remain unimplemented.
